content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Security review - retention controls, audit logs, legal hold (Prospect A x Redwood)
Date: 2025-02-06
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference) [AE]
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Inference) [Product - Security & Compliance]
- Kevin Osei (Redwood Inference) [Security Eng]
- Olga Petrov (Redwood Inference) [GRC]
- Priya Desai (Northbridge Health Systems) [Security Engineering]
- Ben Wallace (Northbridge Health Systems) [GRC / Compliance]
- Lina Chen (Northbridge Health Systems) [Platform]
- Morgan Tate (Northbridge Health Systems) [Procurement]

Auto-summary (generated)
- Northbridge asked for tenant-configurable retention controls across audit logs, admin activity, request metadata, and telemetry/analytics.
- Major focus areas: default retention, minimum/maximum guardrails, proof of enforcement, and legal hold semantics.
- Northbridge needs audit log exports compatible with SIEM ingestion and wants clarity on how exports interact with retention windows.
- Redwood previewed the upcoming “Compliance Reporting Pack” (SOC 2 / ISO-aligned control-to-evidence mapping) and agreed to share a draft.

Topics
1) Data categories & what “retention controls” covers in v1
2) Audit log content, export, and retention boundaries
3) Legal hold: triggers, approvals, and technical behavior
4) Evidence expectations: SOC 2 / ISO style artifacts, testing, and auditability
5) Contract language + procurement questions

Questions (captured)
- Can we set 365 days retention for audit logs while keeping telemetry at 30 or 90 days?
- Do you support “never delete”? If not, what’s the maximum?
- How do you prove deletion actually happened (vs policy config only)?
- How does legal hold override retention? Does it apply per-tenant and per-dataset?
- Can we export audit logs into Splunk/QRadar and still keep a local copy beyond the retention window?
- For Private/VPC, can we run retention enforcement on our schedule / in our region only?

Action items (captured)
- Redwood to send draft compliance reporting pack + control mapping related to retention and audit logging.
- Northbridge to send their internal retention policy table and evidence checklist.

---

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, I think we’re good. Um, thanks everyone for joining. This is the security review slot that Priya requested, focused on retention controls, audit logging, and legal hold. We’ve got Naomi, Kevin, and Olga on from our side.

[00:12] Priya Desai: Yep, thanks Markus. And just to set expectations, we’re mid-review with a couple vendors, including Bedrock and Azure OpenAI as like a baseline. But for Redwood, we’re specifically looking at the deployment flexibility and then the controls around logs and retention.

[00:28] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[00:30] Ben Wallace: I’m Ben, GRC side. I’ll probably ask annoying evidence questions.

[00:33] Olga Petrov: That’s my favorite kind of question.

[00:36] (crosstalk)

[00:37] Lina Chen: Lina here, platform engineering. I’ll ask like “where does it live” questions.

[00:41] Morgan Tate: Morgan procurement. I mostly listen and then I’ll translate to contract asks.

[00:46] Markus Klein: Great. Naomi, do you want to start with a quick framing of what we mean by retention controls?

[00:52] Naomi Feldman: Sure. So, first, we’re rolling out tenant-configurable retention policies for certain classes of data: audit logs, admin activity logs in the console, and selected telemetry/analytics datasets that are tied to operations and usage. For v1 we are not promising full control over every raw infrastructure log stream, like certain managed service logs that have vendor-set limitations.

[01:19] Priya Desai: OK. And when you say “telemetry,” you mean like request logs? Like prompt and response bodies?

[01:26] Naomi Feldman: Good question. No, not prompt/response bodies. In our hosted and dedicated offerings, we treat raw inference payload content as a separate data handling decision. What we’re targeting in this project is request metadata—things like timestamps, model ID, latency, token counts, route, status code, tenant ID—so you can do observability and billing and debugging. Content retention is a later scope item.

[01:54] Lina Chen: So metadata tables, basically.

[01:56] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[01:58] Priya Desai: That helps. Our biggest gap with some vendors is they say “we keep logs 30 days, take it or leave it.” We need to align with our internal policy, which is… it varies. For audit logs we want 365 days. For like operational telemetry, 30 to 90 is fine. But we need the knob.

[02:18] Markus Klein: Yep.

[02:19] Kevin Osei: And just to be explicit, “knob” means per tenant, not global. So one customer can be at 90 days, another at 365, within guardrails.

[02:27] Ben Wallace: Guardrails meaning minimums and maximums?

[02:29] Kevin Osei: Right.

[02:31] Ben Wallace: Do you have those numbers yet or is it “TBD”?

[02:34] Naomi Feldman: We have working defaults. The final min/max is still being finalized, but the shape is: for audit logs, minimum retention is not going to be like “1 day,” because that breaks security and investigations. For most environments we’re targeting a minimum like 30 days. Maximum, we generally don’t allow “never delete” by default in hosted because of cost and risk of retaining forever, but we can do extended windows like 365, potentially longer by contract, and legal hold as an override.

[03:07] Priya Desai: OK, legal hold is the big one for us. We get litigation holds periodically. And we need to be able to preserve logs beyond retention.

[03:16] Naomi Feldman: Yes, that’s a common requirement. In our model, legal hold is an explicit flag that overrides deletion for the held scope.

[03:26] Lina Chen: Scope meaning tenant scope? Like all data types for that tenant?

[03:30] Kevin Osei: It can be per dataset category. In the design we have, a hold can be applied at tenant level and optionally targeted to categories: audit logs only, or admin logs, etc. We avoid holds on “everything everywhere” unless there’s a reason, because it defeats the retention policy and creates noise.

[03:51] Priya Desai: That’s fine. In practice, we’d hold audit logs and admin actions.

[03:57] Ben Wallace: I’m going to ask the evidence question now. How do we prove that a retention policy is enforced? Like, can you show deletion logs, job runs, something we can hand an auditor?

[04:09] Olga Petrov: Yes. The reporting pack we’re preparing includes a control-to-evidence matrix where for retention controls we point to: (1) the configured effective policy per tenant, (2) the enforcement job records—think timestamps, counts, and outcomes, and (3) audit events for policy changes and hold changes. And then we outline a procedure we run internally to generate evidence snapshots on a cadence.

[04:35] Ben Wallace: OK. So there’s an “audit log of the audit log retention.”

[04:39] Olga Petrov: Exactly. Auditors love recursion.

[04:43] Markus Klein: And to keep us grounded, what artifacts are you expecting in your vendor review package? We can line that up.

[04:50] Priya Desai: For security: SOC 2 type 2, pen test letter, and then for this topic, we need a written statement of default retention and configurable ranges, plus legal hold, plus audit log export fields.

[05:06] Ben Wallace: Also: show us how the policy is applied by environment. Like dev vs prod. Because some vendors do weird things.

[05:12] Naomi Feldman: Yeah, we do distinguish. In the policy evaluation, you can have environment-level overrides. So you might have shorter retention in a sandbox environment if it’s non-production.

[05:24] Lina Chen: Is that something we set or you set?

[05:27] Naomi Feldman: By default we set safe defaults. For enterprise tenants, we expose configuration in the Console and via API, subject to RBAC. So your admin can set it.

[05:41] Priya Desai: RBAC… is retention config a separate permission? Like “org admin” only?

[05:47] Kevin Osei: Yes, it’s an admin-level permission. And changes create an admin activity audit event.

[05:53] Priya Desai: Good.

[05:55] Morgan Tate: Can I jump in with a procurement lens? We’ve been burned where a vendor says “configurable,” but it’s “open a ticket.” Do you require a ticket to change retention or can we self-serve?

[06:07] Markus Klein: The goal is self-serve in Console/API. There may be a few constraints where if you want a value outside the allowed range, that becomes a support request and contract addendum.

[06:19] Morgan Tate: OK.

[06:21] Priya Desai: Let’s go deeper on audit logs, please.

[06:24] Markus Klein: Sure. Kevin, do you want to outline what the audit log contains and how export works?

[06:30] Kevin Osei: Yeah. Our audit log captures security-relevant and admin actions within the Redwood platform: console login events, role changes, API key creation/rotation, retention policy changes, changes to routing policies, model pinning changes, and access-related events. Each record has an actor, action type, target, timestamp, and source IP where available.

[06:57] Priya Desai: Do you capture read events? Like someone viewing logs?

[07:01] Kevin Osei: For admin views, we capture access to sensitive settings pages and certain export actions. For “view every log row,” not at that granularity, but for export events and config reads, yes. We can share the field list.

[07:18] Ben Wallace: That’s important. We need to show “who exported audit logs.”

[07:22] Kevin Osei: Yes, export events are captured.

[07:25] Lina Chen: Export mechanism: is it an API endpoint, or you drop a file somewhere?

[07:29] Kevin Osei: In hosted/dedicated, there’s an API and Console export. For larger customers, we also support pushing to customer-managed storage (like S3) or integrating with SIEM via a forwarder. That’s not always “out of the box” for every SIEM, but we have formats that work.

[07:47] Priya Desai: We use Splunk and sometimes QRadar. CSV is fine if the fields are consistent. JSON is better.

[07:54] Kevin Osei: We support JSONL. Also can do compressed archives for larger exports.

[08:02] Priya Desai: Here’s the tricky part: if retention is 365 days, exports should only include what exists, right. But we also want to export daily to Splunk and keep it for like 2 years on our side. Is that allowed? Or do you block export beyond retention?

[08:19] Kevin Osei: We don’t block you from retaining copies on your side. What we do enforce is: if the data is deleted in our system because it’s outside retention and not on legal hold, it’s no longer exportable from us. Exports also include metadata like “export generated at” and we can include the retention window info.

[08:41] Ben Wallace: So you’ll basically say “this export covers Feb 1 to Feb 6, and anything older might have been deleted.”

[08:48] Kevin Osei: Right. And if there’s a legal hold, it changes the effective behavior.

[08:55] Priya Desai: OK. That works.

[08:58] Lina Chen: For Private, do we still get your audit log schema or do we have to implement it?

[09:03] Markus Klein: Private deployment has the same product surface area as much as possible. But the enforcement mechanism can differ depending on customer storage.

[09:10] Kevin Osei: Exactly. In Private, if you’re running in your VPC or on-prem, you can use your own storage and TTL policies. We provide the control plane and the job runners. You can configure retention and holds in the same way; it’s just the underlying “delete job” is running in your environment.

[09:31] Lina Chen: Good, because we have strict data residency. Everything has to stay in us-east-2 or on-prem.

[09:37] Naomi Feldman: Yup. For this call we can keep it to retention, but residency is related: policies can be region-scoped.

[09:44] Priya Desai: Another detail: We need “admin activity logs” separate from “audit logs” sometimes. Like, if someone changed a dashboard, that’s not necessarily audit.

[09:55] Naomi Feldman: In our language, audit logs are security/admin actions. Admin activity may include things like configuration changes in console that aren’t strictly security, but still important. We’ll clarify in the doc. (Sorry, our naming is evolving.)

[10:12] Priya Desai: It’s fine, just define it.

[10:15] Ben Wallace: Also, on SOC 2, we’ll need to map this to CC7-ish controls. Are you providing mapping?

[10:22] Olga Petrov: Yes. The control mapping doc lists SOC 2 common criteria and ISO 27001 Annex A style mappings, with evidence links. For customer-facing, we don’t expose internal links, but we provide a matrix of “control statement -> evidence artifact you can request.”

[10:41] Ben Wallace: Perfect.

[10:44] Markus Klein: Priya, do you want to walk us through your retention requirements at a high level? Like what numbers you need.

[10:50] Priya Desai: Sure. Our policy is: audit logs 1 year online, optionally 2 years archived; system logs 90 days; app logs 30 days unless there’s an incident; and legal hold indefinite until released. For vendor-provided systems, we accept 365 days for audit logs and 30-90 for the rest, provided we can export.

[11:17] Markus Klein: OK.

[11:18] Priya Desai: And we need a documented legal hold workflow: who can set it, how it’s reviewed, and proof it was active.

[11:29] Naomi Feldman: Understood. In our process doc, legal hold changes are auditable, restricted to certain roles, and we have a periodic review requirement so holds don’t linger forever without reason.

[11:45] Morgan Tate: Is that periodic review something you do, or something we do?

[11:49] Naomi Feldman: In hosted/dedicated, we can provide an exception workflow where we ask for justification and set reminders, but the customer is the one with the legal requirement. In Private, you control it.

[12:04] Morgan Tate: OK.

[12:06] Lina Chen: Technical: how do you actually enforce retention? Is it database TTL or a batch job? Sorry, I’m going deep.

[12:13] Kevin Osei: It’s hybrid. Where the datastore supports native TTL/partition expiration, we use it because it’s simpler and less error-prone. Where it doesn’t, we run scheduled deletion jobs that delete in batches with safety limits. We also keep metrics on deletion throughput and error rates.

[12:37] Lina Chen: Safety limits meaning you won’t nuke the DB.

[12:40] Kevin Osei: Exactly. We learned that the hard way in general; so there are backpressure controls.

[12:46] Priya Desai: If you’re using jobs, how do you ensure determinism? Like, we can’t have “sometimes it deletes, sometimes not.”

[12:54] Kevin Osei: We do idempotent jobs with checkpoints. Also, policy evaluation is deterministic: given tenant + dataset + region/environment, you compute effective retention days. Then deletion job uses that computed cutoff timestamp.

[13:16] Ben Wallace: Can you show “last enforcement run”? Like in console.

[13:20] Naomi Feldman: Yes, that’s in the Console UX: effective policy, last run time, last success, errors if any, and holds/exceptions.

[13:32] Priya Desai: Great.

[13:34] Markus Klein: Just to sanity check: is your concern more “can we set retention,” or “can you prove it and explain it quickly in an audit”?

[13:44] Priya Desai: Both. But in practice, the audit story is the thing. We had an auditor last year ask for “evidence of deletion.” And vendors just sent a policy screenshot. That doesn’t cut it.

[13:59] Olga Petrov: Totally. We include evidence that shows not only configuration, but operational logs from enforcement and the system’s behavior under test. For example, we run a test in a non-prod tenant where we ingest sample records, set retention to small value, and confirm they age out, capturing the outputs.

[14:21] Ben Wallace: That’s exactly what we want.

[14:23] Priya Desai: When will the reporting pack be ready?

[14:27] Markus Klein: We have a v1 draft now that we can share under NDA. It’s not a polished PDF for procurement yet, but it’s good enough for your review.

[14:37] Morgan Tate: We have an NDA already, so that’s fine.

[14:40] Markus Klein: Great.

[14:42] Priya Desai: Let’s talk about “never delete.” You said you don’t like it. But our legal hold is essentially “don’t delete.” Is that acceptable?

[14:54] Naomi Feldman: The distinction is “operationally never delete as a default policy” versus “legal hold with justification and explicit activation.” We don’t allow “forever retention” as a casual default because it becomes a data minimization and risk problem. But legal hold exists for exactly your use case.

[15:15] Priya Desai: OK.

[15:16] Ben Wallace: Maximum retention, do you have a number? Like 400? 700? I know it’s arbitrary.

[15:23] Naomi Feldman: For hosted, we’re targeting up to 365 days for audit logs in self-serve. Longer would likely be support/contract. For other datasets, max may be 90 or 180 depending on storage class and performance. We’ll give you the concrete numbers in writing.

[15:44] Ben Wallace: OK.

[15:45] Lina Chen: Can we have different retention for “admin activity” vs “audit log”?

[15:51] Kevin Osei: Yes, that’s the intent: per data type.

[15:54] Lina Chen: And per region?

[15:56] Kevin Osei: Yes where applicable.

[15:58] Priya Desai: Another question: do you log inference requests in a way that includes user identifiers? That’s sensitive for us.

[16:07] Markus Klein: We can configure to avoid PII in logs. But by default, we recommend customers not send PII. In terms of metadata, it’s mostly tenant IDs and request IDs.

[16:18] Priya Desai: OK but we need a statement that you’re not storing prompts by default.

[16:24] Naomi Feldman: Understood. We can provide that statement. We’ll be careful about the exact language because certain features like debugging modes can change what’s captured, but the default posture is not to retain raw content.

[16:42] Morgan Tate: That language should be in the DPA.

[16:44] Markus Klein: Yep, we’ll coordinate with counsel.

[16:47] Ben Wallace: You mentioned “exceptions.” What is that?

[16:50] Naomi Feldman: Exceptions are a controlled way to deviate from standard guardrails—for example, if you need shorter retention for a dataset than our minimum due to internal policy, or longer than max. Exceptions are documented, require approval, and are periodically reviewed. Legal hold is a special type of exception focused on preservation.

[17:16] Priya Desai: Good.

[17:18] Lina Chen: How do you prevent a bad actor from lowering retention to hide their tracks?

[17:24] Kevin Osei: Great question. Controls are: RBAC for who can change retention, audit event for the change, and optionally you can require approval workflow (we’re not shipping full 4-eyes approval in v1, but we can at least provide alerting). Also, minimum retention guardrails prevent dropping to extremely low values.

[17:48] Priya Desai: OK. We might require that any retention change triggers a webhook or something.

[17:54] Kevin Osei: We have audit log streaming and can hook into SIEM, which effectively gives you that.

[18:01] Ben Wallace: So a “retention policy change” becomes an audit event which we can ship to Splunk.

[18:06] Kevin Osei: Exactly.

[18:09] Priya Desai: Nice.

[18:11] Markus Klein: Quick check: are you evaluating other LLM inference vendors besides the hyperscalers?

[18:17] Priya Desai: We looked at Together and Anthropic direct API. The problem is we need private deployment options longer term. That’s why we’re here.

[18:28] Markus Klein: Understood.

[18:30] Morgan Tate: On contract: we usually add language like “Vendor shall retain audit logs for X days and provide export capability.” Would you agree to that?

[18:41] Markus Klein: Typically yes, with specifics. The nuance is: “audit logs” definition and what deployment mode. For Private, you might be the one retaining, so it becomes “platform supports configuring retention,” etc.

[18:56] Morgan Tate: OK.

[18:58] Priya Desai: Can we get a demo of the Console retention page? Or is it not ready.

[19:04] Naomi Feldman: We have wireframes and an early build. We can show you next week. It shows the effective policy, the guardrails, and a banner for legal hold.

[19:15] Priya Desai: Great.

[19:18] Ben Wallace: Another evidence ask: do you have an external audit log coverage statement? Like what actions are included.

[19:26] Olga Petrov: We can provide a coverage summary that lists categories and examples. We need to be careful not to commit to “every single thing,” but we can be explicit about the important ones: auth events, RBAC changes, API key actions, policy changes, export actions, and so on.

[19:46] Ben Wallace: That’s fine.

[19:48] Lina Chen: And you said you can show “last run” of the enforcement job. Are failures visible?

[19:54] Kevin Osei: Yes. We expose status and errors at a high level. Internally we have more detail, but customers will see enough to understand if it’s behind. And there are alerts on backlog.

[20:07] Priya Desai: OK. We need to know if it’s behind because of potential compliance risk.

[20:13] Kevin Osei: Exactly. We’re building monitoring for that.

[20:18] Markus Klein: Priya, can I ask: is the immediate blocker retention, or are there other security items we should anticipate?

[20:25] Priya Desai: Retention and audit logs are the immediate. Secondary is SSO/SAML, but I think you already answered that in the questionnaire. And encryption/KMS.

[20:36] Markus Klein: Yep.

[20:37] Priya Desai: For retention, what’s the timeline? Like when will it be GA.

[20:43] Naomi Feldman: We’re aiming for a staged rollout over the next quarter. For your pilot, we can enable it earlier under feature flag if needed.

[20:54] Priya Desai: That might be necessary. We can’t go to production without it.

[21:00] Markus Klein: Understood.

[21:02] Ben Wallace: Can you clarify which datasets are in v1? Like list them.

[21:07] Naomi Feldman: At a high level: audit logs, admin activity logs, and selected operational telemetry tables. Operational logs “where applicable,” meaning not every infra log. We’ll send the exact list.

[21:23] Lina Chen: “Selected telemetry tables” is vague.

[21:26] Naomi Feldman: Yeah, fair. We’ll give a list with names like request metadata, usage aggregates, and a few tracing indices. But again, no raw prompt content.

[21:38] Priya Desai: OK.

[21:40] (audio glitch)

[21:42] Markus Klein: Sorry, I think we had a blip. Olga, anything else from GRC that you think is important to cover?

[21:48] Olga Petrov: Maybe just the cadence: reporting pack will have a version and a date. We generally update it quarterly or when there’s a major control change. And we can provide a point-in-time snapshot for your audit.

[22:06] Ben Wallace: Great.

[22:08] Priya Desai: One more: For “deletion,” do you do secure deletion? Like cryptographic erasure?

[22:16] Kevin Osei: In general we rely on the underlying storage provider’s deletion semantics and encryption-at-rest. For some stores, deletion means data is removed from active tables; physical media reuse is governed by cloud provider. For Private deployments, you can do your own crypto-erase strategy with keys.

[22:35] Priya Desai: OK. We just need the statement.

[22:39] Morgan Tate: That’s a good example of where contract language needs to match reality.

[22:43] Markus Klein: Yep.

[22:45] Priya Desai: We also need to know if Redwood personnel can access our logs.

[22:51] Markus Klein: Access is restricted, and for enterprise we can do access approvals. Audit logs record admin access. Naomi, do you want to add?

[23:00] Naomi Feldman: In hosted/dedicated, support access is gated and logged, and we can provide an access policy statement. For Private, you control it.

[23:12] Priya Desai: Good.

[23:14] Lina Chen: OK, switching gears slightly. If we set audit log retention to 365 days, does it impact performance or cost?

[23:22] Markus Klein: It can affect cost; we typically price by usage for inference, but retention may have limits by tier. For enterprise, we can include it.

[23:33] Naomi Feldman: From a system perspective, longer retention can increase storage, which is why we have guardrails.

[23:40] Priya Desai: We’re OK paying for it. Just want it predictable.

[23:44] Markus Klein: Understood.

[23:46] Ben Wallace: Another small detail: time zones. Audit logs should be in UTC.

[23:51] Kevin Osei: They are. ISO timestamps.

[23:54] Ben Wallace: Great.

[23:56] Priya Desai: And can we filter by actor, action type, IP, etc.

[24:02] Kevin Osei: Yes.

[24:03] Priya Desai: OK.

[24:05] Markus Klein: I want to be mindful of time. We’ve got about 30 minutes left. What else do you want to drill on?

[24:12] Priya Desai: I want to understand how “effective policy” is computed. Because we have multiple environments.

[24:19] Naomi Feldman: Sure. It’s basically a precedence model: you can have org-level defaults, then tenant-specific overrides, then environment overrides (like prod vs staging), and then region-specific constraints. The system computes a single effective retention duration per dataset per scope, and shows it.

[24:40] Lina Chen: Is it possible for a region to force a longer minimum due to law?

[24:45] Naomi Feldman: More likely a maximum due to data minimization, but yes, we can apply region guardrails.

[24:52] Priya Desai: OK.

[24:54] Ben Wallace: Do you provide an API to fetch effective policy? We’ll want to monitor drift.

[25:01] Kevin Osei: Yes, API endpoint to read effective policy and enforcement status.

[25:07] Priya Desai: Nice.

[25:09] Morgan Tate: You said “feature flag.” Is this something you can enable for us in a pilot, and then later it’s GA.

[25:16] Markus Klein: Yes.

[25:18] Priya Desai: OK. Now, evidence. Can you list what’s in the reporting pack?

[25:25] Olga Petrov: At a high level: (1) a narrative overview of the controls, (2) a retention policy attestation—what’s supported, defaults, guardrails, (3) audit log coverage summary, (4) the control-to-evidence matrix, and (5) a runbook/procedure for how we collect evidence internally, including screenshots and exports.

[25:50] Ben Wallace: That’s what we need.

[25:52] Priya Desai: Will it include screenshots of the console page?

[25:56] Olga Petrov: Yes, likely sanitized.

[26:00] Priya Desai: Great.

[26:03] Lina Chen: I have a practical question. If we do daily exports to Splunk, can we automate that? Or do we need to click.

[26:10] Kevin Osei: Automate via API. Also we have streaming options for audit events.

[26:16] Lina Chen: Streaming is preferable.

[26:18] Kevin Osei: Great, we can set up a technical session.

[26:22] Priya Desai: Another nuance: Some vendors log model outputs as part of “debug logs.” We cannot have that. Is there a guarantee that “operational logs” won’t include sensitive content.

[26:36] Naomi Feldman: The operational datasets in scope are specifically structured metadata. We can provide a statement and list of fields. There may be optional debug tooling where customers can send additional fields, but that would be opt-in.

[26:54] Priya Desai: OK.

[26:56] Ben Wallace: Great.

[26:58] Markus Klein: Anything else on legal hold? I want to make sure we covered.

[27:03] Priya Desai: Yes, legal hold needs: ability to place hold within 24 hours of request; ability to document who requested and why; ability to release; and an audit trail.

[27:17] Naomi Feldman: Yes. The workflow includes who requested, who approved, timestamps, and it’s itself audited. Enforcement jobs check the hold flag and skip deletions in that scope.

[27:33] Lina Chen: Does hold block exports? Like if hold is on, can we still export.

[27:37] Kevin Osei: You can still export. Hold just prevents deletion.

[27:42] Priya Desai: OK.

[27:44] Morgan Tate: And contract: we’ll want a clause that you support legal hold and won’t delete while hold is active.

[27:52] Markus Klein: We can work on that.
